performers: Skidmore College Orchestra, per the Free Music Archive and Internet Archive; not named on the Commons page
question: How can a tune in unequal bars suggest someone walking through a gallery?
intro: Mussorgsky’s walking theme opens the suite and comes back between pictures. No source names the orchestration; this performance has Ravel’s layout of Promenades, so the notes follow his 1922 scoring.

cues.title: The theme alone, then in chords
cues.text: In Ravel’s scoring a solo trumpet states the theme alone, its bars alternating five beats and six. Around 0:08 the melody returns in chords with a brass chorale, and the level jumps by about ten decibels as the strings answer more softly.
cues.evidence: Trumpet solo, brass chorale and softer string reply: Philharmonia listening guide (Joanna Wyld) and LA Phil note (Orrin Howard). The 5/4 and 6/4 bars are in the score. Relative level rises from −15.0 dB at 0:05 to −4.5 dB at 0:10, the loudest window of the first twenty seconds; the report does not identify instruments and estimates 89 bpm, consistent with a crotchet pulse.

cues.title: Slower, darker chords
cues.text: At about 0:28 the sound thins and the harmony darkens towards A♭ and G♭; by 0:40 almost no new attacks are detected. In the piano score an inner note is held while chords and a moving low bass change around it.
cues.evidence: Strongest structural boundary at 0:28 (novelty 1.00). Onsets per second fall from 3.2 (0:25) to 0.0 (0:40); bass pitch class A♭ at 0:30 and F♯ (G♭) at 0:35. The held inner note and moving low bass are in Lamm’s piano score (promenade-1.ly); no bar alignment is claimed.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Hartmann is boiling
cues.text: Around 12 June 1874, writing to Vladimir Stasov, Mussorgsky reported that “Hartmann is boiling as Boris boiled”. He finished the whole suite in three weeks, between 2 and 22 June, within a year of Viktor Hartmann’s death.
cues.evidence: Letter to Stasov, probably 12 June 1874, quoted in Wikipedia’s Pictures at an Exhibition article (composition history); LA Phil and Boston Symphony notes give the composition dates and Hartmann’s death. The note sits over a quiet passage (−22.6 dB at 0:55).

cues.title: Broad chords hold the level
cues.text: From about 1:10 the sound stays within a few decibels of its maximum, with few new attacks per second. Chords carry the tune above a walking bass, the broadest statement in the movement.
cues.evidence: Relative level is −9.3 to −6.4 dB across 1:10–1:35 at 0.4 to 1.6 onsets per second; the loudest windows are 1:15, 1:25, 1:30 and 1:35.

cues.title: Stasov’s picture of the walker
cues.text: Vladimir Stasov described the opening as Mussorgsky “roving through the exhibition, now leisurely, now briskly”, sometimes thinking sadly of his dead friend. The score marks the last chord attacca, running straight into Gnomus.
cues.evidence: Stasov’s programme quoted in Michael Steinberg’s Boston Symphony note (https://www.bso.org/works/pictures-at-an-exhibition); attacca mark in Lamm’s score (Mutopia). The level falls to −33 dB at 1:40.

transitions.title: Lower parts enter; the harmony darkens
transitions.how: The statements so far end in the F and A♭ regions. At about 0:28 the lower parts re-enter and the harmony darkens towards A♭ and G♭; chords change slowly while an inner note is held and the bass moves. Activity drops sharply. The melody keeps its rising shape and its unequal bars, so the new texture is the same walk taken more slowly, not a new subject.
transitions.evidence: The strongest boundary in the report is 0:28 (novelty 1.00); onsets per second fall from 3.2 at 0:25 to 1.2 at 0:30 and 0.0 at 0:40, and the bass pitch class moves to A♭ (0:30) and F♯/G♭ (0:35). The held inner note, moving bass and chord layout are from Lamm’s piano score; the match to the orchestral version is by proportion only.

transitions.title: The chords lift and F major returns
transitions.how: The slow chords give way to a bass that steps down and up again, and the music arrives in F major, the dominant of B♭, with a jump in loudness. From here the tune is carried by full chords. The harmonic route is a retransition by bass motion, not a modulation: the closing bars return to B♭ major.
transitions.evidence: Boundary at 0:44 (novelty 0.90); relative level rises from −19.4 dB (0:40) to −8.9 dB (0:45); local key reads F major from 0:45 (r 0.67–0.93) and B♭ major at 1:40 (r 0.92). Key labels are confirmation only; the bass motion is from the score’s second half.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Orchestral performance; Ravel’s 1922 orchestration is the probable version but is not named by any source
fields.note: Neither Commons, the Free Music Archive nor the Internet Archive names the orchestrator. The album’s four Promenades (none between “Samuel Goldenberg and Schmuÿle” and Limoges) match Ravel’s layout, and a 2015 Commons talk-page comment calls the recording Ravel’s orchestration of a rather poor Skidmore performance. The commenter gives no source. Instrument names in the listening notes follow Ravel’s scoring conditionally, as the introduction says; the audio report does not identify instruments.

fields.value: Mussorgsky’s piano suite (he died in 1881) is public domain; Commons marks the music PD-old-100. An orchestration is a separate work with its own term and is not cleared here.

composer.epithet: He made Russian speech, public crowds and the noises of ordinary life determine the shape of opera.
facts: Piano with Anton Gerke; composition informally with Mily Balakirev; no conservatory education
Guards officer until 1858; civil servant, including work in the Forestry Department
Balakirev, Borodin, Cui and Rimsky-Korsakov; the critic Vladimir Stasov
Operas, dramatic songs and piano music; many works unfinished or published in other composers’ revisions
composer.background:
Mussorgsky grew up on his family’s estate at Karevo, where his mother taught him the piano and his nurse supplied stories that he later associated with his earliest improvisations. The household belonged to the landowning class. The peasant voices he eventually put into songs and operas came from another social world. Sent to Saint Petersburg for schooling, he studied piano with Anton Gerke and entered the School of Guards Cadets in 1852. In 1856 he joined the Preobrazhensky Regiment. His first published piano piece, a polka, belonged to the drawing room.

Meeting Dargomyzhsky and then Balakirev redirected that education. Balakirev taught through playing, criticism and the examination of scores. Mussorgsky left the army in 1858, but composing did not provide a living. The emancipation of the serfs in 1861 disrupted the estate income on which his family depended, and he eventually took civil-service posts. The group later called the Five brought together different professions and musical methods: Borodin was a chemist, Cui a military engineer, Rimsky-Korsakov a naval officer. Their shared opposition to imported academic authority concealed substantial musical disagreements.
